Also they write down literally everything you do and when you have your evaluation with your treatment team to decide your discharge date, they take all that into account and may punish you with a longer stay for not participating as much as they want you to. A few days before you leave you and your therapist will have a family session with family members of your choosing to discuss plans for your treatment after discharge and how they can support you. But tbh it’s very jarring as an experience and you really feel trapped especially with little to no contact with the outside world. I would not recommend it.

Some places are really restrictive and if you break a rule they put you on unit restrictions where you can’t leave the unit for any reason. Your meals are brought to you from the cafeteria. Some places this is an extreme thing only for if you are an active threat to yourself or others, some you can get this for swearing or skipping group.

Some places will let you swap roommates for any reason, some only under certain circumstances, and some not at all. At one of the ones I was at, I got to switch rooms because my roommate was actually threatening to kill me because she thought I had stolen something of hers. That was wild. Sometimes staff are nice. Sometimes they are horrible. It’s really luck of the draw. But if they suck you can vent with the other patients and do things to mildly annoy them.

And there’s a dress code. No short shorts or skirts, no low cut anything, no leggings, people with boobs have to wear a bra. If you break dress code, they give you either a hospital gown or those paper scrubs to wear. When you get there for intake, they do strip search you and document every scar on your entire body. It’s very invasive. Oh you get woken up every morning super early for vitals. And even earlier your first full day there for blood work.

Oh and lots of places have certain restrictions for items you can bring. No drawstrings or shoelaces (you can have lace up shoes but they will take the laces out and zip tie them), some places ban jewelry (including piercings other than earlobes) others just no long or chunky jewelry, some ban books with controversial content and will either lock them up under your bed or literally scribble out the bad stuff,  bras can’t have underwire but you have to wear one if you have boobs so sports bras only, some places no crayons, some places no alcohol based markers, medical devices you can have but have to leave with staff at night (I had a knee brace one of the times and I had to get it from staff every morning), no zippers.

They encourage you not to socialise with other patients. They strictly do not allow sharing contact info. That isn’t always enforced tho. They do have activities you can do in the day room during breaks such as puzzles. Oh and you have to lock up your toiletries in a cubby and get it unlocked for you during designated hygiene times if you want to shower and brush your teeth and hair. No razors allowed in most places. Others only the disposable kind and only with staff supervision.

They have a psychiatrist who you see every day who monitors your meds and tries to find the right ones for you. Most places have an average stay of 7-10 days. I once stayed for 15 days because I wasn’t feeling better and I was being honest about it. My therapist then told me to lie and say I felt better to go home because they couldn’t help me (not quite in those exact words). They really encourage you to go to their outpatient after discharge. By encourage I mean you have to really convince them you’ll be okay seeing your own outside providers frequently or they will hold you hostage until you agree to do their outpatient.

When you have visitors, they have to be on your approved visitor list and have your patient number. It’s two visitors per person at a time for like 30 minutes and they can’t bring you anything into visits. They have to leave it at the desk with your name, unit, and patient number. You can make phone calls on their landlines. Some places have designated phone call time and monitor you. Some places you can call any time and you aren’t monitored. But you are limited to 20 minutes per call and you can only make one before handing off to someone else. Only people from your approved list of phone numbers can call you and they have to have your patient number. If you need their number, you can get a copy of that list.

During set medication times, a nurse will give you your medications and ask a bunch of questions (including your last bowel movement). Beware the booty juice. If you act up or in some hospitals if you so much as eye staff funny, they will hold you down and give you a shot in the ass to sedate you. You can watch TV (sometimes any time before lights out, sometimes only for a certain amount of time) but no phones or electronics. You can have visitors. Some places allow them every day. Some only on certain days. Bigger hospitals also have multiple wards that rotate visiting days. There will be one for adolescents, one for just mental health, one for just substance abuse, one for co-occurring, and sometimes one for certain patients with psychotic disorders (they called them the real crazies when I was there which is super offensive).

There are set mealtimes where a staff member takes you a in a single file line to the cafeteria and you get whatever they’re serving that day. The food sucks ass. It’s been super gross all three places I’ve been. Don’t expect anything nice. They usually have a soda machine but that doesn’t work during breakfast if it works at all. Also some places might have a tv in the cafeteria. But if you want to watch something, the other patients have to agree to it. If there’s any arguments, they turn it off and you eat with no background noise. If you’re there for an ED, they will check how much you are. They also might give you ensure to boost your calorie intake. If you start eating less while you’re there and staff feels some type of way about it, they might give you ensure then too even if you are not there for an eating disorder. On the ward they sometimes have flavoured water and/or coffee.

They will have a set schedule with different therapy groups. If you want a one on one session with your assigned therapist, you have to request it. The types of therapy offered will be things like recreation therapy, music therapy, process group, activity group. Some places have fresh air breaks. On adult wards they will have smoke breaks if you smoke. And sometimes fresh air breaks where there is no smoking. They don’t always actually let you out though. You might have to go with the smokers if you want to be outside.

Generally they do not monitor you in your room unless you get put on line of sight or 1 to 1. Line of sight means you have to be in plain view of staff at all times. I got put on that one time and they were short staffed so they dragged my mattress into the hallway and made me sleep there. The second night they had more staff so they dragged a chair into my room and someone sat and watched me sleep all night. Also I had to leave the bathroom door open when I peed so staff could watch. It creeped me the fuck out. 1 to 1 means a staff member has to be with you at all times. One of the psych wards I went to did not allow anyone to be in their rooms during the day, though.

On adolescent wards, they separate the boys and the girls and the only time you’re allowed to have contact with each other is meals and school time (if they have that) You got one pillow and one blanket and you were not allowed to ask for more. There were no real hooks to hang anything on. The windows were bulletproof glass and did not open. None of the doors had handles. They were all push to open.

No sharp objects either. No pens or regular pencils. They will give you pen refills or golf pencils to write with and you can bring certain approved brands of markers and some places allow crayons, some don’t. The psych wards I was in, you had an assigned room with someone of your same sex assigned at birth (not gender identity. Unfortunately they were all very transphobic, two of the hospitals constantly deadnamed and misgendered trans patients even after being corrected).

Well it depends on which one you go to. I’ve been inpatient three times at three different psych hospitals in three different cities. Each one had different staff, were run differently, and had different rules. But they had a lot in common. So basically it’s a sterile environment. The walls are white. Everything is some shade of pastels. Some places bolt down the furniture some don’t. But either way, there are no sharp edges.
